title: N-S-A
hook: nasa: to lift, to carry, as in Naso

segments.voice: Yesterday, A-R-V: erev, evening, and arev, the one who stands surety. Your line was we stand surety. The priestly blessing had its own day back on day four hundred thirty-nine; today's root does its lifting.

When the Torah counts people, it doesn't always use a word for counting. In the portion called Naso, God tells Moses: "Take also the sum of the sons of Gershon." The Hebrew is naso et rosh: lift up the head. To count someone, in that phrasing, is to raise their head, to see each face, one at a time. Later in the same portion comes a blessing that lifts something else: "The LORD lift up his countenance upon thee, and give thee peace." Today's root does the lifting in both.
screen: `NASO: LIFT UP THE HEAD.` → `EACH FACE, ONE AT A TIME.` → `LIFT UP HIS COUNTENANCE.`

segments.voice: N-S-A. Nun, sin, alef. Nasa: to lift, to carry, to bear. First, the eyes. "I will lift up mine eyes unto the hills, from whence cometh my help." I will lift is essa, from this root. Lifting begins with where you look. Second, the shoulders. In the same portion, Naso, the Levites of Kohath carry the holy things of the sanctuary, and the text says they bore them upon their shoulders: the same verb. The leaders of the tribes in that portion are called nesi'im, from these letters too. Third, forgiveness. When God's attributes are proclaimed to Moses, one of them is "forgiving iniquity and transgression and sin." The Hebrew for forgiving there is nosei: carrying. To forgive, in this root, is to lift a wrong off someone and bear it. Cain uses the same verb from the other side, in despair: "My punishment is greater than I can bear." Too heavy to lift. Fourth, the hands. When the priests bless the people with the words from Naso, the practice is called nesiat kapayim, the lifting of the hands. So one root raises heads to be counted, eyes to the hills, holy things onto shoulders, wrongs off backs, and hands in blessing. In this root, lifting and carrying and forgiving are one motion.
screen: `I WILL LIFT UP MINE EYES.` · `HOLY THINGS ON THEIR SHOULDERS.` · `FORGIVING IS CARRYING.` · `THE LIFTING OF THE HANDS.` · then, large: `ONE MOTION: LIFT.`

segments.voice: Let your shoulders rise on an in-breath and drop on the out-breath, a few times, slowly. Then ask what someone near you is carrying that you could lift a little, a chore, a worry, a grudge you could set down, or choose a weight of your own to put down for now. If you pray, you can say the psalm's line: I will lift up mine eyes unto the hills. And if something ever feels too heavy to bear alone, please reach out: in the US, call or text 988, any hour; elsewhere, local emergency help.
screen: `SHOULDERS UP, SHOULDERS DOWN.` · `WHAT COULD I LIFT?` · `CHOOSE ONE.`

segments.voice: N-S-A. Nun, sin, alef: nasa, to lift, to carry, to forgive. And this week's lines, in order: the world hides, exile reveals, sit and learn, friendship joins, dawn, we stand surety, lift. Today's word.
Your line: lift. Eyes first, then shoulders, then hands. Same time tomorrow.

howItsDone: The Torah portion Naso (Numbers 4:21–7:89) takes its name from 'naso et rosh', lift up the head; it includes the priestly blessing, which the priests give with raised hands, nesiat kapayim. Exodus 34:7 uses the same verb for forgiving.

chat.says: How can the same Hebrew word mean both lifting and forgiving?
options: To forgive, in this root, is to lift a wrong off someone and carry it.
It can't; they're two different roots that only look alike.
Forgiving means lifting your hands in blessing over the person who hurt you.
